source.title: Scaling Laws for the Principled Design, Initialization and Preconditioning of ReLU Networks

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Its displayed title, “Beyond Folklore: A Scaling Calculus for the Design and Initialization of ReLU Networks,” differs from the supplied title.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares initialization schemes and reports training-loss outcomes, addressing initialization’s effect on optimization speed. It does not measure the training classification error named by V1.
record.gate_note: The study reports training-loss comparisons for initialization schemes on 26 LIBSVM datasets and CIFAR-10. Its Hessian scaling analysis and activation second-moment calculations are not separate training outcomes. Prior-work claims about very deep orthogonal networks are cited, not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares early training loss under different ReLU initialization and scaling schemes, testing V4's training-speed component. It does not test greater trainable depth or the orthogonal-versus-Gaussian claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors propose scaling as a practical guide to designing networks that stochastic gradient methods can optimize, while acknowledging that it is not a universal solution.
record.recipe_differences: Compares geometric-mean initialization and scaling with arithmetic-mean, fan-in, and fan-out initialization; the experiments compare training loss and do not directly measure classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scheme changes the reported loss; on CIFAR-10, the geometric-mean scheme's advantage over fan-out is limited to mid-iterations.

fits_no_version.finding: Unnormalized ResNet-50 reaches ImageNet test accuracy 76.18 (SE 0.04), versus 76.13 (SE 0.03) for RescaleNet across five seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric initialization and scaling can match RescaleNet's final test accuracy in an unnormalized ResNet-50. This comparison does not measure initialization-dependent training speed, depth degradation or normalization's speed benefit.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 comparison is described with training-loss curves but the text provides no exact curve values. The LIBSVM results aggregate across datasets and do not state per-dataset uncertainty or outcomes in the table.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying training-loss results were left out. Hessian singular-value and second-moment analyses characterize initialization scaling, not a separately reported training outcome; cited results about very deep orthogonal networks were not tested in this study.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and model-size, early-stopping and regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious-local-minimum frequencies and extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation and plain-versus-identity-shortcut comparisons.

Greater trainable depth, activation-function comparisons, very deep tanh networks, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and 10,000-layer convolutional training. The experiments establish comparative early convergence, not a causal demonstration that preventing signal or gradient explosion explains it.
Initial stability thresholds, loss catapults, curvature evolution and edge-of-stability training.
Training speed or learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, and Fixup comparisons.

missing.what: Dataset heterogeneity deserves explicit result rows: fan-out is best on 12 datasets, worst on nine and sometimes fails to learn; geometric initialization is best on six and worst on none. Aggregate losses alone conceal these differences.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4. Its results support initialization-sensitive convergence without establishing a universal ranking of initialization schemes. The limited advantage over fan-out does not warrant a limits_scope verdict on V4.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and the effects of model size, early stopping, and regularization are not measured.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem or bad-local-minimum frequency sweep.

The study compares geometric-mean, arithmetic-mean, fan-in, and fan-out initializations for ReLU networks, but does not test the initialization schemes or 10,000-layer trainability claims specified in the version.
No learning-rate stability-limit or sharpness-threshold experiment.
No batch-normalization comparison or Fixup experiment.

rows.subject: 3-weight-layer non-convolutional ReLU network
rows.size_stated: Inner-two layer widths fixed at 384 and 64 nodes; 3 weight layers total.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with arithmetic-mean initialization; median loss after 5 epochs aggregated across 26 LIBSVM datasets.

conditions.value: 10 seeds per dataset, learning rate, and initialization

rows.measure: Average normalized training loss after 5 epochs
rows.locator: Table 2: Comparison on 26 LIBSVM repository datasets
rows.note: The paper reports this as the arithmetic-mean initialization result; it does not provide dataset-level values in the table.
rows.check: The value is correct. Interpret jointly with R2–R4 as an initialization comparison; nonzero normalized loss does not imply a partial effect. Each dataset and initialization uses its best swept learning rate. Losses are divided by the worst initialization's loss within each dataset before averaging.

rows.subject: 3-weight-layer non-convolutional ReLU network
rows.size_stated: Inner-two layer widths fixed at 384 and 64 nodes; 3 weight layers total.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fan-in initialization; median loss after 5 epochs aggregated across 26 LIBSVM datasets.

conditions.value: 10 seeds per dataset, learning rate, and initialization

rows.measure: Average normalized training loss after 5 epochs
rows.locator: Table 2: Comparison on 26 LIBSVM repository datasets
rows.note: The paper reports this as the fan-in initialization result; it does not provide dataset-level values in the table.
rows.check: The value is correct. Together with R1, R3 and R4 it shows initialization-dependent early convergence, rather than a partial effect inferred from absolute loss. The baseline and learning-rate selection should be recorded as described for R1.

rows.subject: 3-weight-layer non-convolutional ReLU network
rows.size_stated: Inner-two layer widths fixed at 384 and 64 nodes; 3 weight layers total.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fan-out initialization; median loss after 5 epochs aggregated across 26 LIBSVM datasets.

conditions.value: 10 seeds per dataset, learning rate, and initialization

rows.measure: Average normalized training loss after 5 epochs
rows.locator: Table 2: Comparison on 26 LIBSVM repository datasets
rows.note: The paper says fan-out is often best but sometimes completely fails to learn; its average loss is worst on 9 datasets.
rows.check: The value is correct. It is comparative evidence of initialization-dependent convergence. The aggregate conceals strong dataset variation: fan-out is best on 12 datasets and worst on nine, with complete learning failures reported for some problems.

rows.subject: 3-weight-layer non-convolutional ReLU network
rows.size_stated: Inner-two layer widths fixed at 384 and 64 nodes; 3 weight layers total.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with geometric-mean initialization; median loss after 5 epochs aggregated across 26 LIBSVM datasets.

conditions.value: 10 seeds per dataset, learning rate, and initialization

rows.measure: Average normalized training loss after 5 epochs
rows.locator: Table 2: Comparison on 26 LIBSVM repository datasets
rows.note: The paper reports geometric initialization has the lowest average loss and is never the worst of the four methods on any dataset.
rows.check: The lowest average early loss supports the training-speed component; it should not be marked partial merely because loss remains nonzero. Geometric initialization is best on six datasets and worst on none. Widths 384 and 64 were deliberately chosen to amplify differences.

rows.subject: Strided AlexNet architecture
rows.operation_detail: Compared geometric-mean initialization with arithmetic-mean and fan-in initializations on CIFAR-10.

conditions.value: Geometric learning-rate sweep; figure reports preconditioned and arithmetic at 0.05, fan-in at 0.1, and fan-out at 0.05

rows.measure: Minibatch training loss over 400-step sliding windows
rows.value: Preconditioning is a statistically significant improvement over arithmetic-mean and fan-in initialization (p = 3.9 × 10−6).
rows.note: The text says the advantage over fan-out appears only at mid-iterations. The figure shows medians and 25%-75% IQRs, but no exact loss values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The significant training-loss improvement is observed. Describe the intervention as geometric initialization plus fixed scaling, rather than weight initialization alone. All methods receive fixed output scaling to initial standard deviation 0.05, and learning rates are swept separately.

rows.subject: Strided AlexNet architecture
rows.operation_detail: Compared fan-out initialization with the other initialization schemes on CIFAR-10.
rows.measure: Minibatch training loss over 400-step sliding windows
rows.value: The geometric-mean initialization only shows an advantage over fan-out at mid-iterations.
rows.note: No exact losses are stated in the text; medians and 25%-75% IQRs are displayed in Figure 3.
rows.check: The reported geometric-over-fan-out advantage is confined to mid-training. Make geometric preconditioning the subject if retaining that comparison direction; the current subject and value point in opposite directions. This timing restriction does not itself qualify V4, which does not promise geometric initialization always beats fan-out.

relationships.condition: Three-weight-layer ReLU networks on 26 LIBSVM datasets, after five epochs and with separately selected learning rates
relationships.reason: R1–R4 show initialization-dependent early convergence: average normalized losses are 0.90, 0.84, 0.88 and 0.81, with geometric initialization lowest.
relationships.display_finding: Average normalized losses were 0.90, 0.84, 0.88 and 0.81 across tested initializations, with geometric initialization lowest.

relationships.condition: Strided AlexNet on CIFAR-10, with controlled initial output scale and swept learning rates
relationships.reason: R5 reports improved training loss over arithmetic-mean and fan-in initialization (p = 3.9 × 10−6); R6 shows an advantage over fan-out during mid-training.
relationships.display_finding: Geometric initialization improved training loss over arithmetic-mean and fan-in initialization with p = 3.9 × 10⁻⁶, and outperformed fan-out during mid-training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Geometric initialization had the lowest average normalized loss, 0.81, and was never worst across the 26 datasets (R1–R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The text reports a significant advantage over arithmetic-mean and fan-in initialization, but says the advantage over fan-out appears only at mid-iterations (R5–R6).
